To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

successful task performance is associated with task-induced deactivation in the prefrontal, cingulate, parietal and temporal brain regions in younger adults, and older adults with or without mild probable AD.

Task-induced deactivations, as measured by fMRI, during successful paired associates memory performance, increase in magnitude with increasing task difficulty in younger adults, older adults, and older adults with mild probable Alzheimer's Disease (AD).
task-induced deactivating brain regions were observed during successful paired associates encoding and retrieval in young and old adults, and in old adults with and without probable AD.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the functional role of task-induced deactivation in the context of age and Alzheimer's disease.

a better understanding of the role of the prefrontal cortex, anterior cingulate, posterior cingulate and other brain regions in the successful encoding and retrieval processes of paired associates in younger and older normal adults as well as older adults with and/or without AD.
the neural substrates of successful paired associates learning in younger and older healthy adults and in older adults with mild probable AD.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
task-induced deactivatory activity is a common phenomenon across the life-span and in healthy aging, and in the early stages of AD.
the task-induced deactivating pattern observed in younger, healthy older adults and older adults with AD was not affected by AD, but by task difficulty and age.
task-induced deactivation is a function of task difficulty and age but not AD.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the pattern of task-induced deactivation in older adults is similar to that in younger adults and is not affected by mild AD.
task-induced deactivation in the medial pre- and cingulate regions is related to the level of task demand.
task-induced deactivatory responses are preserved in AD and that these responses are not significantly altered in AD patients compared to healthy older adults.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the magnitude of task-related deactivations in the medial frontal and posterior cingulated regions increases with the difficulty of the task, and that these regions are affected by aging, but are relatively preserved in mild AD.

the pattern of task-induced deactivation observed during successful encoding and recall of paired associates in younger adults is also observed during successful performance of the task in older adults and AD patients.
task-induced deactivatory activity, which is associated with successful task performance, is preserved across the lifespan and in AD.
